Figure 2:Overview of OneSteer.1Body-group reference features and proprioception
condition the controller.2A one-step generator predicts a state–action plan.3Task costs steer the generator input with weights
fixed.4An inverse-dynamics head computes the current command
from near-term planned states, current feedback, and the reference.
The controller replans at the next step.
Lower panels summarize the two training routes and body-group
handover (tracking: model trained from scratch, BONES; tasks:
distilled model, second call steered).
Plan renderings are simulated; hardware experiments
evaluate nominal tracking and SDF-based steering.

Figure 3:Steering moves the plan.Four time steps (left to right) of one rollout under a 1.25 m bar. Top: unsteered; grey ghosts show the 0.96 s plan, red marks planned poses that hit the bar, and gold is the reference. Bottom: the same reference with test-time steering; the plan (blue) ducks under the bar and the robot executes it. Weights, reference and executor are unchanged.

Figure 4:Failure assessment from noise spread.TheKKplans fromKKnoise inputs (colored ghosts) for the same
reference and state, no simulation.
Left: the plans agree and the scoreSSis low.
Right: the plans scatter andSSis high.

Figure 5:Steering on a physical Unitree G1with an SDF cost built from the onboard LiDAR and the same frozen policy throughout. Left: unsteered, the head hits the bar and knocks it off; steered, the robot lowers early, passes under, and walks out to stand. Right: unsteered, the foot catches the hurdle and the robot falls; steered, the robot raises each foot and steps over.

Figure 6:The same frozen policy without (top) and with (bottom) a test-time cost(simulation; one clip each, same reference; earlier poses in grey without and blue with steering). Over the test sets, steering raises knee-fault survival from 0.71 to 0.79, halves ball loss (0.16 to 0.08) and lowers the VR wrist error from 24.3 to 16.4 cm.

Figure S1:Nominal tracking on a physical Unitree G1.Representative frames from nine whole-body motion sequences.
The overhead tether is an unweighted safety guard.
Figure S2:Highly dynamic motions on a physical Unitree G1, tracked by OneSteer without steering: two backflips and a run (time from the first frame of each row).

Figure S3:Steering on the robot over time(same frozen policy and walking reference in all rows; LiDAR distance field). Low bar at 1.1 m: unsteered, the head hits the bar and knocks it off; steered, the robot lowers and passes under. Hurdle of 12 cm: unsteered, the foot catches the hurdle and the robot falls; steered, the robot raises its feet and steps over.

Figure S4:Steering over time in simulation(same frozen policy and reference in each pair of rows). Colors as inFig.S5: the executed robot in grey, the plan as ghosts (red where it hits the obstacle, blue after steering), the reference in gold. Unsteered, the plan runs into the low bar and over the hurdles, and the robot falls at the hurdles; steered, the plan lowers the body under the bar and lifts the feet over each hurdle, and the robot follows it.

Figure S5:Plan ghosts before and after steering.Four time steps of one rollout each (left to right), for a hurdle (top two rows) and a low bar (bottom two rows). For each scene, the upper row is unsteered: grey ghosts show the 0.96 s plan, red marks plan poses that hit the obstacle, and gold is the reference motion. The lower row is the same reference after test-time steering (blue ghosts).

Figure S6:One terrain-conditioned model on five terrain families(simulation). Each panel overlays four poses, about 0.55 m apart, of one rollout (earlier ones in blue); the reference is on flat ground, and the policy sees the terrain only through the height-scan tokens.
